# Substance Use and Pain Curriculum Innovation: Establishing a Student-Faculty Partnership for Curricular Change

**Authors:** Rory Vu Mather; Helen E. Jack; Katherine E. Warren; Cameron Comrie; Sienna Li; Michael Liu; Erika Lynn-Green; Sydney Moore; William Oles; Shahin A. Saberi; E.J. Jarvie; Anjali Koka; Patrick McGuire; Antje M. Barreveld; Hilary S. Connery; Todd Griswold

**Affiliations:** Harvard–MIT Program in Health Sciences and Technology, Boston, Massachusetts | Department of Medicine, University of Washington School of Medicine, Seattle, Washington | Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts | Department of Anesthesia, Harvard Medical School, and attending physician, Department of Anesthesiology, Critical Care, and Pain Medicine, Boston Children’s Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts | Department of Psychiatry, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts | Department of Anesthesiology, Tufts University School of Medicine, Boston, Massachusetts, and attending physician, Department of Anesthesiology, Newton-Wellesley Hospital, Newton, Massachusetts | Division of Alcohol, Drugs, and Addiction, McLean Hospital, Belmont, Massachusetts, and assistant professor, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts | Center for Mindfulness and Compassion, Cambridge Health Alliance, Cambridge, Massachusetts, and director, Medical Student Education in Psychiatry, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts

## Abstract

The opioid overdose crisis had progressed broadly in the United States, with an 21% increase from 2016 to 2017, and specifically in Massachusetts, with a peak rate of 1,374 deaths in 2016. In 2016, students and faculty at Harvard Medical School (HMS) established the Substance Use and Pain Curriculum Committee (SUPCC) to expand substance use and pain education. However, faculty capacity, financial resources, and administrative support were insufficient to implement changes across all phases of the medical school curriculum.

The HMS SUPCC restructured in 2021 to put students at the forefront of curricular development. This restructuring was done through 3 main innovations: (1) establishment of a student-centered committee structure, ensuring that curricular changes are centered on student interests and needs; (2) student-led curricular development and implementation, reducing faculty workload; and (3) focus on clinically relevant teaching and opportunities to practice learned skill sets.

This student-centered structure facilitated the expansion of the addiction and pain medicine curriculum to more than 30 hours of teaching by 2024. Examples of student-driven initiatives include development of an opioid use disorder management practicum equivalent to the Drug Enforcement Agency X-waiver, increased medical student access to naloxone through a hospital partnership, and integration of case-based opioid use disorder and pain medicine didactics into the clerkship year.

Although this work has established a longitudinal curriculum across all medical training stages, more must be done in clerkship rotations to help students apply their substance use and pain education in the clinical setting. The HMS SUPCC is working to incorporate teaching on nonopioid substances, such as alcohol, cannabis, and ketamine, provide longitudinal clinical experiences so students learn to care for patients with substance use disorder and chronic pain from short-term intervention to long-term recovery, and develop surveys to quantitatively and qualitatively measure curriculum outcomes.

## Problem

In 2016, the opioid overdose crisis had rapidly progressed both broadly in the United States and specifically in Massachusetts (Figure 1). Drug overdose deaths in the United States increased 21% from the year prior, the largest annual increase recorded at that time.1 Synthetic opioids, such as fentanyl, became the leading cause of opioid-related overdose deaths.1 In Massachusetts, deaths reached a peak of 1,374 deaths in 2016, 75% of which involved fentanyl.2 Boston faced a compounding crisis when the sudden closing of its largest homeless shelter in 2014 left hundreds of patients disconnected from safe housing and substance use disorder (SUD) treatment. That year, then Massachusetts Governor Charlie Baker met with the deans and faculty members of the 4 Massachusetts medical schools to develop core competencies for the prevention and management of inappropriate use of prescription drugs.3 It was this combination of a national trend in overdose deaths, a severe crisis in Boston, and state-level political advocacy that motivated Harvard Medical School (HMS) to establish the Substance Use and Pain Curriculum Committee (SUPCC) in 2016.

The original HMS SUPCC consisted of 19 members: medical students, faculty across multiple departments, and medical education leadership. Many of the student members were drawn from an existing student activist group, the Student Coalition on Addiction, which was founded in 2014 by medical students in response to the closure of Boston’s largest homeless shelter.4 The SUPCC’s initial goal was to establish a required substance use and pain curriculum that spanned all phases of the curriculum. We incorporated Miller’s5 pyramid of clinical competence to inform curricular developments, which guides students through a progressive journey beginning with the acquisition of fundamental knowledge and progressing to hands-on engagement with patients. Using this educational framework, the SUPCC developed a substance use and pain curriculum in 2016 approved by the HMS Curriculum Cabinet (Table 1), the body responsible for the oversight of the medical school curriculum. A more detailed overview of our curriculum with the corresponding HMS competencies and Miller’s pyramid of clinical competencies is shown in Supplemental Digital Appendix 1 (at [WK INSERT LINK]). In its first 5 years, our committee updated foundational teachings in SUP topics in the preclinical curriculum.

However, as we transitioned our focus in 2021 toward providing opportunities to put that knowledge into action during clinical clerkships, we realized that our group lacked the faculty bandwidth, financial resources, and administrative capacity to implement clinical teaching. These challenges forced our group to consider how we could restructure our efforts to focus faculty time on key curriculum content updates and advocating for institutional support. Given the long history of student advocacy in the creation of the HMS SUPCC, in 2021 our committee started the process of exploring how we could establish a larger role for students, freeing up faculty time for institutional advocacy and high-level curricular input. In this article, we describe how we established a horizontal leadership structure among students and faculty and how this accelerated our curriculum innovation in substance use and pain.

## Approach

In 2021, the SUPCC restructured to establish a horizontal leadership structure among students and faculty. We now have 2 committee leads: an overall faculty lead chosen by HMS administrators and a student lead chosen by student committee members. The 2 work together to establish the committee’s mission, goals, and projects. We also have 2 faculty subleads in charge of overseeing core content within our 2 themes: substance use and pain medicine. This shared leadership structure allows faculty to focus their efforts on areas where expertise is vital for curricular development, while centering student perspectives.

Medical students of all years apply to join the committee on an annual basis, regardless of their experience with addiction and pain medicine. General student members can individually or in groups choose a project to pursue and are assigned a faculty mentor from the committee, who provides guidance on the content and format for the project. Examples of projects have included creating a focused lecture on core substance use and pain topics incorporated into the preclinical curriculum, an interactive case-based session during clerkship rotations to teach how to put substance use and pain knowledge into clinical practice, or initiatives to distribute harm reduction resources to students and patients, such as naloxone. The students for each project progress through their work independently of committee meetings, reporting to the larger committee for feedback and assistance with implementation.

We have 2 sets of committee meetings: student working group meetings focused on the details and timelines of specific projects and full-committee meetings focused on committee-wide projects and individual project feedback. This scheduling structure cuts meeting obligations for faculty in half and focuses their efforts on providing necessary expertise.

The student-led committee structure helped SUPCC overcome several key challenges to the implementation of the curriculum. To characterize the implementation context of our curricular changes, we used the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research.6 The combination of a public health crisis and state mandate (outer setting) and long-standing student advocacy for additional training (inner setting) facilitated rapid faculty and institutional leadership engagement in curriculum development. However, several inner-setting factors presented barriers. First, substance use and pain topics span multiple medical specialties and are not consolidated into a single course. Therefore, the SUPCC could not access the same resources as course faculty, such as funding, administrative support, and faculty development. It also left the decision to incorporate our teachings into courses in the hands of individual course directors. Second, faculty were usually only affiliated with one of the Harvard-affiliated teaching hospitals, making it difficult for them to coordinate didactics with other teaching sites.

Some of these inner-setting barriers were alleviated when our institution created societal themes that focused on priorities for curricular development in response to the Liaison Committee on Medication Education accreditation introducing standard 7 (curricular content) and element 7.5 (societal problems).7 Our committee’s long-standing history of student advocacy led to substance use and pain education being chosen as one of the societal themes at HMS, providing the financial support for our faculty leads, legitimacy, and access to curriculum stakeholders to affect our curricular changes. We also realized that students could help mitigate the obstacles of distributing our didactics to all parts of the medical school curriculum and across all teaching hospitals because they work across hospitals in a way that faculty do not. Students can highlight the opportunities and limitations students have on a medical team during clerkship rotations within a specific hospital, connect our committee with the clerkship directors and instructors they meet during rotations, and provide feedback on how didactics fit into existing curricula. This process also provides students with the opportunity to develop their teaching skillsets, receive one-on-one mentoring with faculty, and contribute to academic publications and conference presentations.

## Outcomes

### Student and faculty engagement

After implementing our student-centered structure in 2021, the SUPCC increased its student membership from 2 students in 2020 to more than 20 in 2024. Students expanded the number of active projects from 1 or 2 at a given time to more than 7 concurrent projects. The opportunity to engage in medical education scholarship helped motivate student engagement: in the 2023 to 2024 academic year the SUPCC published 2 articles, submitted 2 manuscripts for peer review, gave an oral conference presentation, and had 3 conference poster abstracts accepted. The action-based didactics created through student projects transformed our addiction and pain medicine curriculum from covering the basics of SUD treatment and pain management to more than 30 hours of didactics spread across the medical school curriculum (Table 2). Below we describe 3 of the student-led initiatives incorporated into our substance use and pain curriculum.

### Buprenorphine prescribing

When we first began to outline areas in the curriculum that covered substance use and pain topics, students pushed to take this one step farther to see if the curriculum could satisfy the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) X-waiver requirements to prescribe buprenorphine for opioid use disorder (OUD). Students and faculty created a medication for OUD practicum that was incorporated into the postclerkship curriculum. This practicum includes asynchronous prework reviewing foundational teaching on medication for OUD and a 2-hour in-person didactic with 4 interactive patient cases spanning age, gender, and special populations. This practicum, combined with preclerkship addiction training, provided sufficient training for students to meet requirements for their DEA X-waiver. As of 2024, more than 600 students in 4 graduating classes had received X-waiver equivalent training. Although recent changes in X-waiver requirements no longer necessitate this training, these didactics remain in the curriculum because the DEA maintains required OUD and SUD training.

### Access to and training on naloxone rescue

Before the inception of the committee, students from the Student Coalition on Addiction had led efforts for naloxone to be included in basic life support training for each medical student.8 However, when students went to their local pharmacy to procure doses to distribute to the medical school as part of the Massachusetts standing prescription order, they were hindered by supply shortages and cost-prohibitive price tags for over-the-counter kits. Students on the SUPCC worked with the outpatient pharmacy at an affiliate teaching hospital to establish an expedited pathway for medical students and residents to obtain naloxone processed through insurance and shipped directly to their homes.9 This pathway was established in 2022 and as of 2024 has distributed 150 doses of naloxone to medical students and 150 to residents and hospital staff.

### Case-based acute pain management training

Despite the presence of foundational teaching on pain medicine, the curriculum lacked education on practical aspects of pain management in clinical scenarios. In 2024, we introduced didactics in both the core medicine and surgery clerkships to prepare students to provide effective pain management across a variety of clinical scenarios. In the core medicine clerkship, we developed a primer on the various forms of medical pain management, enabling students to engage more critically in discussions about optimal pain regimens. We have also created an interactive case aimed at providing students with the fundamentals of OUD epidemiology, diagnosis, and management with an emphasis on harm reduction. Four pilot sessions for this didactic conducted from February to October 2024 included more than 30 clerkship students, and validated assessments completed before and after the sessions demonstrated significant improvement in knowledge about managing acute pain in patients with OUD, identifying examples of harm reduction, and counseling patients on medication for OUD. For the core surgery clerkship, our team developed an interactive case session taught in small groups to review different methods of acute pain management used by the perioperative team.

### Next Steps

During the 3 years after our restructuring in 2021, the SUPCC deployed a student-centered approach that allowed us to develop curricular improvements that extend beyond knowledge acquisition and into clinical practice. The primary innovation of our work, however, is the student-led model of curriculum development, an implementation strategy that helped overcome several institutional implementation barriers while providing important learning and career development opportunities for students. We believe this curriculum and change-making process can serve as a blueprint for other medical schools on how they can establish workflows where students and faculty work as peers to bring about lasting and impactful curricular improvements.

The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration released a report in April 2024 outlining a core curriculum on SUDs for medical education programs.10 Through the efforts of our committee, the HMS has already incorporated many of the suggested topics and championed their push to include students as stakeholders in curricular change.

Although our work has established a longitudinal curriculum across all stages of medical training, we believe more must be done in clerkship rotations to help students apply their substance use and pain education in the clinical setting. Students are working to incorporate teaching on nonopioid substances, such as alcohol, cannabis, and ketamine. We are also developing longitudinal clinical experiences so students learn to care for patients with SUD and chronic pain from short-term intervention to long-term recovery. We are working to develop surveys to quantitatively and qualitatively measure the outcomes of our curriculum, including the acquisition of core knowledge in addiction and pain medicine, preparedness of graduating medical students to treat patients with SUDs and chronic pain, and the number of students pursuing careers with a focus in addiction and pain medicine.

# Clinical Impact of 3- Vs. 5-Minute Delay and 30- Vs. 60-Second Intervals on Unattended Automated Office Blood Pressure Measurements

**Authors:** Erika E Lynn-Green; Jennifer L Cluett; Ruth-Alma N Turkson-Ocran; Kenneth J Mukamal; Jonathan X Li; Stephen P Juraschek

**Affiliations:** Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | Division of General Medicine, Department of Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | Healthcare Associates, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

## Abstract

Guidelines advise automated office blood pressure (AOBP) with an initial 5-minute delay and multiple measurements at least 60 seconds apart. Recent studies suggest that AOBP may be accurate with shorter delays or intervals, but evidence in clinical settings is limited.

Patients referred to 1 hypertension (HTN) center underwent 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) and 1 of 4 nonrandomized, unattended AOBP protocols: a 3- or 5-minute delay with a 30- or 60-second interval, i.e., 3 min/30 s/30 s, 3/60/60, 5/30/30 and 5/60/60 protocols. HTN was defined as systolic blood pressure (SBP) ≥140 or diastolic blood pressure ≥90 mm Hg.

We compared differences in mean blood pressure and HTN classification between average AOBP and awake-time ABPM by t-tests and Fisher’s exact test. Among 212 participants (mean 58.9 years, 61% women, 25% Black), there was substantial overlap in the probability distributions of awake-time ABPM and each of the 3 AOBP measures. SBP means were similar between the 5/60/60 and 3/30/30 protocols and 5/30/30 and 3/60/60 protocols. The 5/30/30 was associated with a higher proportion of systolic HTN, while the 3/60/60 protocol was associated with a higher proportion of diastolic HTN. There were no significant differences in systolic or diastolic HTN between 5/60/60 and 3/30/30 protocols with respect to awake-time ABPM.

In this quality improvement study, the shortest AOBP protocol did not differ significantly from the longest protocol. The time savings of shorter protocols may improve AOBP adoption in clinical practice without meaningfully compromising accuracy.

Blood pressure (BP) measurement is one of the most frequently performed clinical assessments, and the quality of measurement profoundly affects the detection and management of hypertension.1 The body of literature in support of hypertension screening and treatment is based on high-quality, standardized BP assessments.2,3 In particular, automated office BP (AOBP) with at least 2 measurements is increasingly recommended to improve both accuracy and precision in the clinic.4,5 However, to date, few outpatient clinics have adopted standardized AOBP protocols. One commonly cited barrier to implementing AOBP is the time required for patients to rest before and between replicate measures. We hypothesized that accurate and precise AOBP might be achieved with a shorter time delay and interval, but evidence is lacking.

Guidelines recommend an initial delay of 3–5 minutes before the first BP reading at a given visit6,7 with strong support from observational evidence showing profound changes in BP when taken later in the visit, presumably after the initial stimulus of arriving at the clinic has subsided.8 This was recently challenged by 2 randomized trials, showing that no rest before unattended AOBP more accurately reflected awake ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM),9 and yielded identical seated BP results to a 5-minute rest in an attended design.10 However, some have questioned the generalizability of these trials to clinical practice based on key departures from the typical patient experience, e.g., performing measurements after an informed consent process9 or conducting the study in a nonclinical setting with a standardized activity period.10

Current guidelines also recommend intervals of 1–2 minutes between AOBP readings7,11 based in part on trial protocols.9,10 While we recently reported that 30-second intervals yield equivalent results to 60-second intervals, this was only examined after a 5-minute delay.12 It is unclear if a reduced initial delay, in addition to shorter intervals between measurements, will have a greater impact on measurement accuracy. Along these lines, one study noted that the difference between the first and third measurements was most important for diagnosing hypertension, as these measurements are directly influenced by rest time and the duration of the measurement period.13

In this factorial design, quality improvement study performed in a general medicine hypertension clinic, our objectives were to compare patients’ mean awake-time ABPM with the mean of 3 AOBP measurements obtained (1) after a 3- vs. 5-minute delay or (2) with a 30- vs. 60-second pause between cuff deflation and the next inflation cycle. We hypothesized that the shortest AOBP protocol (i.e., a 3-minute delay with a 30-second pause) would be equivalent to the longest protocol (i.e., a 5-minute delay with a 60-second pause), and these effects would not differ by delay or pause interval (i.e., no interaction between the 2 factors).

## METHODS

### Population

We tested 2 different delay times with 2 different pause interval times for unattended AOBP among patients of the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC) Hypertension Center at Healthcare Associates (where patients are referred for complex HTN management) between 15 April 2021 and 29 June 2023. As a quality improvement initiative, the BIDMC Institutional Review Board determined this project to be exempt research (see Supplementary Material 1 for details). The study began in the spring of 2021, with the plan to enroll 100 patients: 50 with a 5-minute delay and 60-second pause as an interval and 50 with a 3-minute delay and 60-second pause interval. In January 2022, in response to practice-wide changes to adopt a 30-second interval between BP measurements, the investigative team increased the scope of the quality improvement project to include an additional 100 patients using a 30-second pause interval (i.e., about 50 with a 5-minute delay and 30-second pause interval and 50 with a 3-minute delay and 30-second pause interval). Protocol was designated in advance by month, such that patients with appointments within a given month underwent the protocol assigned for that month. The final schedule for performing protocols may be found in Supplementary Table S1. Analyses were restricted to the patients (N = 212) who completed all BP assessments. Protocols were conducted using the SpaceLabs 90227 or 90217A-1 ABPM (Spacelabs Healthcare, Snoqualmie, WA) and the Omron HEM-907XL (Omron Healthcare, Lake Forest, IL), both with validation studies published previously.14

### Ambulatory BP measurement

Patients referred for ABPM underwent a standardized BP measurement protocol as follows. On day 1, patients were brought to a private exam room where a tape measure was used to measure the circumference of their mid-arm to determine cuff size; when available, cuff sizes were confirmed using the range indicators printed on the cuff (Spacelabs or Omron). BP measurements were performed using the nondominant arm unless there was a medical contraindication such as tremor, prior mastectomy, or continuous blood glucose monitor.

Patients were then fitted for ABPM, which they wore for the following 25 hours. Patients then took off the monitor and returned the device 1–2 days later during a follow-up visit. ABPMs were preprogrammed to measure BP every 20 minutes during awake hours and hourly during sleep hours based on patients’ self-reported sleep/wake times. When the device was actively measuring, patients were asked to remain still and let their arm rest on their other arm, on an adjacent table, or at heart level. Participants were given a log for sleep times, awake times, and relevant activities (such as exercise, meals, timing of medications, driving time, and periods when the monitor was removed) during the 25-hour period. The actual sleep and awake times were used to determine the average awake ABPM. The majority of participants had over 20 successful awake ABPM readings. Notably, there were only 2 patients with less than 20 measurements while awake (N = 18 and 19, respectively).15

### Unattended AOBP measurement

Unattended AOBP readings were performed every time during the visit when the ABPM device was returned (day 2 or 3, depending on the date of ABPM placement). An additional day between ABPM and AOBP measurements was introduced due to an unrelated clinic schedule change on 16 May 2022. No changes were made to patients’ hypertension medication regimen from the 7 days prior to the ABPM monitoring period through the follow-up visit in the clinic. Patients were assigned to 1 of 4 AOBP timing protocols by month based on a prespecified schedule (Supplementary Table S1): 5-minute delay and 60-second pause intervals (N = 67, “5/60/60”), 3-minute delay and 60-second pause intervals (N = 51, “3/60/60”), 5-minute delay and 30-second pause intervals (N = 50, “5/30/30”), 3-minute delay and 30-second pause intervals (N = 44, “3/30/30”).

Patients underwent an unattended, preprogrammed 3- or 5-minute delay followed by 3 BP measurements (designated M0–M2), separated by a 30- or 60-second pause interval. Before measurement, clinic staff were trained to position patients with their feet on the floor, backs supported, palms facing upright, and cuffs placed on bare skin. Arms were elevated at heart level and supported on a table. Signage was posted outside the clinic room to minimize noise and interruptions. The monitor display did not display BP readings during measurements. Staff left the room after starting the monitor and returned after the third measurement was complete.

We defined stage 2 or uncontrolled hypertension as a systolic blood pressure (SBP) ≥140 mm Hg and/or diastolic Blood pressure (BP) (DBP) ≥90 mm Hg, following the National Committee for Quality Assurance’s Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set definition for uncontrolled BP. Compliance with this metric is used as a benchmark for quality, linked to financial incentives for clinical practices. This definition was of primary interest to our clinic in this quality improvement project.

### Other covariates

Demographic information on age, sex, and race were obtained from the medical record. As part of clinical care, patients were asked about prior diagnoses of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, sleep apnea, current antihypertensive and cholesterol-lowering medications, smoking status, and alcohol use. The most recent available data on body mass index and creatinine were obtained from the medical record. We also tracked patients’ reason(s) for referral (new diagnosis of hypertension, uncontrolled hypertension, white coat hypertension, orthostatic symptoms, or other).

### Statistical analysis

Population-level characteristics were assessed using both overall means and proportions and according to the 4 protocols. Bland–Altman plots were used to visualize differences between the mean AOBP by protocol. We calculated the mean and SD for SBP and DBP by measurement type according to each protocol, as well as the prevalence of stage 2 or uncontrolled hypertension (SBP ≥140 mm Hg and/or DBP ≥90 mm Hg) according to each protocol. All means and proportions used mean awake-time ABPM as a reference. Means were compared using paired t-tests and reported as mean differences; proportions were compared using the McNemar χ2 test. Root-mean-square errors were determined for each measurement. We produced Lowess curves and scatter plots displaying the means of AOBP and ABPM for every patient by date of visit to evaluate any trends over time given the clinic setting (Supplementary Figure S1).

We calculated differences between each AOBP measurement and awake-time ABPM, using generalized estimating equations (normal family, identity link, robust variance estimator) to model the mean value at each measurement. We also examined how differences in measurements differed by protocol. In addition, we determined the performance of the distinct protocols for identifying patients with SBP ≥140 mm Hg and/or DBP ≥90 mm Hg via area of the curve, sensitivity, specificity, positive likelihood ratio, and negative likelihood ratio. This was repeated in supplemental analyses for SBP ≥130 mm Hg and/or DBP ≥80 mm Hg.

We also used linear regression to examine the association of the 4 AOBP protocols with each BP measurement adjusted for age, sex, and race (model 1) or additionally adjusted for the difference between the first automated measurement and awake-time ABPM in Supplemental analyses (model 2). In addition, we examined whether the association between each measurement and awake-time ABPM differed across each study protocol compared to the 5/60/60 protocol via protocol-by-BP measurement interaction terms adjusted for age, sex, and race (model 1) or additionally adjusted for the difference between the first automated measurement and awake-time ABPM in supplemental analyses (model 2) as described above. These comparisons were repeated using logistic regression with respect to the classification of stage 2 or uncontrolled hypertension (SBP ≥140 mm Hg and/or DBP ≥90 mm Hg). In sensitivity analyses, we reanalyzed data by factorial design (3- vs. 5-minute delay or 30- vs. 60-second interval) due to the presence of an interaction between delay and intervals.

All statistical analyses were performed using Stata 15.1 (StataCorp LP, College Station, TX). A 2-tailed P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

### Factorial analysis

There was evidence of interaction by delay and interval protocols in relation to SBP for the first AOBP measurement; thus, we examined factorial contrasts in sensitivity analyses. Baseline characteristics were generally balanced across factors (Supplementary Table S2). Moreover, measurement distributions and means were roughly similar between the 5- and 3-minute delays and the 60- and 30-second intervals for both SBP and DBP (Supplementary Figures S3 and S4; Supplementary Table S8). There was no evidence that a 3- vs. 5-minute delay or a 30- vs. 60-second interval was associated with higher odds of hypertension (Supplementary Table S9). Moreover, there was no evidence that AOBP measurements (individually or averaged) associated with awake-time ABPM differently across factors (Supplementary Table S10).

## DISCUSSION

This quality improvement study of over 200 patients investigated the real-world performance of various unattended AOBP protocols in a clinic setting compared to awake-time ABPM. Overall, our results indicate that the shortest AOBP protocol, with a 3-minute initial delay and 30-second pause intervals between measurements, was statistically equivalent to the longest protocol with a 5-minute delay and 60-second intervals. Moreover, there were no major differences in the associations between individual AOBP measurements and awake-time ABPM regardless of delay and interval settings.

AOBP is an important tool for high-quality BP measurements in the clinic setting, which remains a crucial environment for diagnosing and managing hypertension.4,16 However, AOBP uptake has been low, motivating inquiry into whether a shortened time interval might yield BP measures with similar accuracy and precision as longer AOBP protocols used in prominent clinical trials.17,18

Recent randomized trials showed that a shorter delay compared to a 5-minute delay had no impact on BP measurements.9,10 However, one of these trials was attended in a research environment,10 in which BP measurements are known to differ from clinic environments.19 While the other trial was performed unattended in a clinic setting, patients underwent a consent process prior to participation, which likely entailed a semi-rested period in the seated position.9 Many describe the logistic challenges and rush to appointments as a stressful patient experience that may alter BP. One large study showed significant reductions in BP between the first and second BP measurements in the clinic.8 In contrast, our study was performed in a typical office setting with usual intake procedures.

The longest protocol, 5/60/60, had average SBP and DBP AOBP readings that did not significantly differ from the shortest protocol, 3/30/30. This was true for each individual AOBP measurement (M0, M1, and M2) as well as for the mean of M1 and M2 (excluding the first reading) and the overall mean of all 3 readings. Furthermore, the shortest protocol did not compromise the accuracy of BP measurement compared to the longest protocol. In hypertension classification, the proportion of patients with an AOBP mean SBP over 140 mm Hg or DBP over 90 mm Hg who had an ABPM mean under these cutoffs also did not significantly differ between the longest and shortest protocols. This was consistent across both the absolute proportions of hypertension classification compared to ABPM and for the odds of classifying a patient as hypertensive compared to the longest protocol.

Multiple guidelines recommend 1–2 minutes between BP measurements20,21 based on a few studies showing minimal differences between 1- and 2-minute intervals.22,23 However, data comparing measurements with shorter time intervals are limited. Imamura and colleagues found similar performance between measurements with 30- and 60-second intervals.24 Our previous work in a distinct group of over 100 patients found that a 30-second interval was statistically equivalent to 60 seconds in the clinic setting following a 5-minute delay.12 The present study examined this question after a 3-minute delay, showing similar accuracy and precision between shorter and longer intervals regardless of the initial delay. Another important consideration is the sequence effect, which has been well-described and has been a major rationale behind discarding the first measurement when assessing BP.25–27 Later measures may be especially influenced by a shorter interval. Nevertheless, we did not observe consistent differences across protocol assignments even after discarding the first measurement.

In our analysis, an interaction effect between delay and interval was present with respect to SBP from the first AOBP measure, affecting the factorial analysis; however, the reasons for this are unclear and were potentially by chance. This is supported by the observation that an interaction involving measurement 1, could not be influenced by the pause interval. In addition, a close examination of protocol assignments did not reveal any consistent pattern of bias. In fact, the most discordant pairings, 5/30/30 and 3/60/60 as well as 5/60/60 and 3/30/30 were the most alike. These differences were likely not physiologic but should be the focus of further work.

This study has limitations. First, patients were not randomized in our study but were assigned to an AOBP protocol a priori on a month-by-month basis, possibly introducing confounding factors not accounted for between groups. Nevertheless, baseline characteristics were balanced across the 4 protocols. Second, practice staff and procedures changed over time. As the interval comparison was added later in the 2-year study period, there could be temporal effects on measurement performance and the patient population. However, to account for this, we intentionally repeated the 5/60/60 assessment throughout the study. Moreover, the means of AOBP and ABPM were reassuringly consistent across the study period. Third, while our study included over 200 people, no power calculations were performed prior to the study’s commencement, and therefore, the findings should not be interpreted as definitive. It should also be noted that there may be differences and variability in the training and implementation of AOBP by staff, which could reduce our ability to detect differences. Nevertheless, fluctuation in staff training and practice is reflective of real-world settings. Fourth, it is possible that performing AOBP after ABPM would lead to an order effect as patients would be acclimated to BP readings, although AOBP readings were still higher than ABPM on average, and this order effect was consistent across the protocols. Nevertheless, randomizing patients into distinct orders would allow for a better comparison of AOBP to ABPM. Fifth, the clinical importance of attended vs. unattended BP measurements is an ongoing debate; it is unclear whether our results might differ when attended.28–30 Sixth, our study looked at both BP measurement and the classification of BP ≥140/≥90 mm Hg. While measurement did not differ consistently between protocols, the traditional approach classified adults with BP ≥140/≥90 mm Hg most similarly to ABPM. It is possible that devices may perform differently at different ranges of BP, which should be a focus of subsequent work. Seventh, we were not able to examine the effects of medication use and did not collect details of concurrent antihypertensive class as part of this study, which should be examined. Last, BP variability between visits is greater than measurements within-visit.31 The impact of a shorter within-visit protocol on between-visit BP variability remains an important question for subsequent research. Nevertheless, the discordance between AOBP and awake-time ABPM observed in our study supports recommendations to base clinical decisions on more than one visit, as within-person differences are not the same as group differences.

Our study has clinical implications for providers taking BP measurements in outpatient settings and potential implications for guidelines related to AOBP. AOBP was very similar to awake-time ABPM, demonstrating the value of this form of measurement in the clinic setting. However, the adoption of AOBP, already recommended for BP measurement quality improvement, has been limited in part due to concerns related to perceived time requirements. In our investigation, measurement accuracy and precision did not differ significantly between the longest (7 minutes) and the shortest protocols (4 minutes). Three minutes of rest time saved per patient is substantial for busy clinic environments. Time savings with similar accuracy suggested by these findings could promote AOBP uptake and optimal BP measurement for every clinic patient. Importantly, our findings reinforce reports from recent trials9,10 that a shortened rest period is acceptable for AOBP without compromising its accuracy in a real-world context, addressing concerns about the generalizability of these prior works to clinical care.

In conclusion, while several areas remain to be further investigated, in this clinic-based quality improvement study, the shortest AOBP protocol reduced time without compromising BP measurement accuracy or HTN classification compared to the longest protocol. These results support the implementation of more time-efficient AOBP in clinical practice.

# Variations in how medical researchers report patient demographics: a retrospective analysis of published articles

**Authors:** Erika E Lynn-Green; Avery A Ofoje; Robert H Lynn-Green; David S Jones

**Affiliations:** aHarvard Medical School, 25 Shattuck Street, Boston, MA 02115, USA | bThe Medical University of South Carolina, 171 Ashley Avenue, Charleston, SC 29425, USA | cMathematica Inc., 1100 First St NE #1200, Washington, DC 20002, USA

## Abstract

The use of demographic variables in the medical literature has been a topic of much recent debate. Recent studies found that race and socioeconomic status (SES) are inconsistently reported. Best-practice use of sex and gender has been contentious. We aimed to characterise the state of medical demographic reporting in greater detail, especially regarding geography and specific terms used in articles.

Original articles were included from issues of the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM), JAMA, The Lancet, and the American Journal of Epidemiology (AJE) published from 1 January to 31 December 2020 (n = 640). Articles without human participants, case reports, or with only aggregate data were excluded, leaving 594 articles. Use of age, sex, gender, race, ethnicity, and SES were coded, as well as corresponding author and participant geography.

99.0% of articles reported age. While 92.9% reported sex alone, only 4.7% used the term gender and 1.0% transgender. 47.8% of articles reported race and 29.6% reported ethnicity. Studies with U.S. corresponding authors or participants were significantly more likely to report race (72.9% and 73.7% respectively) or ethnicity (47.3% and 45.3% respectively) than those without (25.9% and 25.6% for race, 14.2% and 16.3% for ethnicity), p < 0.01 for all. Of articles reporting race, 40.9% used only a Black-white binary; of those reporting ethnicity, 85.2% included two or fewer terms. Under 5.0% of all articles used Office of Management and Budget (OMB) categories. Across all articles, 33.0% reported SES, from 15.2% in NEJM to 80.2% in AJE.

We found that while some factors (age, sex) are reported consistently, others (gender, race, ethnicity, SES) are not, despite recent attention. Authors often rely on binary or limited categories that inadequately capture human diversity. The presence of U.S. researchers or participants increased the reporting of race and/or ethnicity, highlighting wide variations that persist even as multinational collaborations become widespread. Researchers should reflect on their use of these terms, justify their decisions, and report results with care.

## Evidence before this study

We searched for “race,” “ethnicity,” and “socioeconomic status” with “demographics medical literature” on Google Scholar on 14 November 2020 and identified fourteen studies that showed that race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status (SES) were under- or inconsistently reported across medical journals, largely in specialty-specific literature. An additional literature search on 10 January 2023 revealed four papers published in the interim that found similar results in major medical journals.

## Added value of this study

To further clarify current practices and identify possible targets for reform, we examined in detail the descriptive statistics of a broader set of articles with greater attention to the specifics of demographic terms and how usage varied across researchers and participants in different countries, novel contributions to the literature. We based our study on an analysis of the two highest impact US medical journals, NEJM and JAMA, with high-impact comparisons also novel to the literature: a UK journal (The Lancet) to enable broader geographic comparisons and an epidemiology journal (AJE) to explore whether disciplinary standards differed.

## Implications of all the available evidence

The decisions that researchers make about what to report reflect their judgments about what really matters, and inform the judgments that others make, potentially with regrettable consequences. Researchers need to reflect on their use of sex, gender, race, ethnicity, and SES, to justify their decisions when they do so, and to report results with care.

## Introduction

All clinical research faces a basic question: can results derived from one group of people be applied to others? To help clinicians determine this, researchers report baseline characteristics of their study population, from age and sex to risk factors, comorbidities, and medical care. Efforts to characterise patients precisely and comprehensively have become increasingly important with growing interest in both personalised medicine and the social determinants of health.

Policies about best practices for the collection and reporting of demographic descriptors, which have been debated for decades, have become increasingly controversial. The 1993 U.S. NIH Revitalization Act, which sought to increase the inclusion of women and minoritised groups in clinical research, asked researchers to examine whether sex, gender, race, or ethnicity mattered in their analyses and, if so, to report data by these categories.1 U.S. researchers were advised to follow the categories defined by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB): five races (American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian, Black or African American, Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander, or White) and two ethnicities (Hispanic or Latino, or not).2 The data standard for sex was simply male or female.2

Researchers continue to debate when and how such categories should be used, in medicine and in society more widely.3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 Is race a reflection of ancestry and genetics, a social construct, a product of racism, or all of those things? Do the OMB categories capture the complexity of human diversity and identity? Different countries parse diversity differently, with different expectations and requirements for researchers.11 This is increasingly relevant as international collaborations and multi-sited studies become widespread.

Recent evidence has found that race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status (SES) are still under- or inconsistently reported across major journals.12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20 Labels for sex (referring to biological characteristics) and gender (referring to sociological characteristics) have also become contentious, with calls to standardise and clarify their use in academic settings as the rising visibility of sexual and gender minority patients has exposed the inadequacy of a male-female binary variable.21, 22, 23 Furthermore, researchers now recognize the profound impact of socioeconomic status (e.g., income, education, insurance status, etc.) and exposures (e.g., environmental, racism, structural violence, etc.) on health and treatment outcomes.24, 25, 26 Despite this, neither federal funders nor journal editors have defined best practices for the use or reporting of SES variables.27,28

To further clarify recent practices and identify possible targets for reform, we examined in detail the descriptive statistics used in articles in three top medical journals and one top epidemiology journal, paying particular attention to the specifics of what terms were used, and how. We also examined how usage varied across researchers and participants in different countries, a novel contribution to the literature. Many recent studies have focused on journals in a specific specialty. We chose instead to examine the most highly-read medical literature and analysed the two highest impact US medical journals, the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM) and Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA). We then pursued two high-impact comparisons: a UK journal (The Lancet) to enable broader geographic comparisons, and an epidemiology journal (the American Journal of Epidemiology, AJE) to explore whether and how disciplinary standards differed.

We undertook a retrospective analysis of published articles from 1 January to 31 December 2020 in NEJM, JAMA, Lancet, and AJE. Meta-analyses were included if they reported data on patient demographics. This process yielded 594 original articles (Fig. 1; Table 1).

### Data analysis

We analysed what information each article included about age, sex, gender, race, ethnicity, or SES. If this was not reported in a table, we searched the text for any occurrences of relevant terms (Supplemental Table S1). Each article was coded to indicate whether specific variables—age, sex, gender, race, ethnicity, SES—were reported (e.g., the variable was present or absent). If a variable was reported, we noted the specific language used. We also recorded the geographic locations of the corresponding authors and participants, as noted in the article or elsewhere (e.g., clinicaltrials.gov). Initial data collection and analysis was undertaken by E.E.L., A.A.O., and R.H.L. The coding of each article was then additionally checked by the senior author D.S.J., with all data therefore verified by two authors. We developed policies to address ambiguous cases and assign geographical authorship (Supplemental Appendix 1); these were resolved by the first author E.E.L.

We calculated the percentage of articles that reported each variable across all four journals and for each journal. We also calculated percentages according to geography based on whether the corresponding author (an imperfect proxy for where the research was centred) was in the U.S., and whether any of the research participants resided in the U.S. Chi-squared tests for geographical comparisons were performed by E.E.L. using R Studio, Version 1.2.5033.

Institutional review board approval was not required as no human participants were involved. No funding was obtained.

## Results

Nearly all articles (588, 99.0%) identified the age of the research participants, typically reporting the mean age in each group (Table 1, Fig. 2).

Nearly all articles (580, 97.6%) reported sex or gender (Table 1, Fig. 2). Most of those articles (552, 92.9%) reported sex alone, almost exclusively as male-female. Only 28 (4.7% of all articles) used “gender”; most of those (23 of 28) did not distinguish “gender” from “sex,” used “gender” in place of “sex,” or used it interchangeably with “sex” (Fig. 3a). Only 6 articles (1.0% of the total) used “transgender”; five of those articles focused explicitly on sexual and gender minority research participants or questions. We could not determine how the other 588 studies handled transgender participants.

Race was specified in 284 articles (47.8%) and ethnicity in 176 (29.6%) (Table 1). These are an overlapping set: 312 (52.5%) reported race or ethnicity, 157 (26.4%) reported both, 127 (21.4%) reported race alone, and only 19 (3.2%) reported ethnicity alone (Fig. 3b). Of the 157 that reported both, only 52 (33.1%) separated them as distinct categories (Fig. 3b). Specific language varied widely (Table 2). Of the 284 articles that reported race, 133 used two or fewer terms, usually a Black-white (or Black-non-Black) binary (116 articles, 40.9%). Of the 176 articles that reported ethnicity, 150 (85.2%) included two or fewer terms, usually Hispanic or not. Of the 312 articles that reported race or ethnicity, 204 (65.4%) also included an undefined “other” category. Only 18 articles (3.0%) used the exact language of the OMB categories, and only 24 articles (4.0%) mentioned the OMB categories in any form, including with some categories combined.

The use of categories for race or ethnicity varied significantly with geography (Fig. 4, Table 3). Assessing the geography of the publications was complex, because of the high prevalence of articles that listed both U.S. and non-U.S. authors (255, 42.9%) and the challenge of assessing the intellectual home of the project. Thirty-five unique countries were represented in the affiliations of corresponding authors, with country-level proportions reporting age, gender or sex, race or ethnicity, or SES presented in Table 3. Five corresponding authors reported two country affiliations; for the analyses in Table 3, their articles were categorised under both countries. Articles with U.S. corresponding authors were by far the most prevalent at 277, with the U.K. (70), Canada (42), China (25), and Australia (20) filling out the top five countries by articles published. U.S.-affiliated articles reported on race or ethnicity far more frequently than articles from other countries (Table 3, Fig. 4).

Across all articles, 196 (33.0%) reported a variable that reflected SES. Specific usage (i.e., about reporting education, income, or insurance) ranged widely, as did answer options (Table 2). There were notable differences in how many articles reported SES among the journals, ranging from 32 (15.2%) in NEJM to 28 (21.2%) in Lancet, 51 (34.9%) in JAMA, and 85 (80.2%) in AJE (Fig. 2). Geographic differences were less pronounced than with race and ethnicity but still statistically significant (Table 1, Fig. 4): an SES variable was included in 112 (40.4%) of articles with a U.S. corresponding author and 84 (26.5%) of articles without a U.S. corresponding author (χ2 = 12, p < 0.01). One hundred and three (37.6%) articles with U.S. participants vs. 93 (29.1%) of articles with non-U.S. participants reported SES (χ2 = 4.5, p = 0.03). Almost all AJE authors who reported race or ethnicity also reported an SES variable (55; 85.9%). This was not the case in JAMA (39; 47.0%), NEJM (19; 17.7%), or Lancet (9; 15.5%).

## Discussion

Our results show that race, ethnicity, and SES variables continue to be reported at low rates, and that these variables, along with sex and gender, are often used indistinctly or without clear definition. Moreover, we saw wide variations in these practices by researcher and participant geography, which suggests that cultural or socio-political considerations influence how these variables are used. These results complement and expand on recent findings that the reporting of race, SES, and sex remained limited in the medical literature and had not statistically changed between 2015 and 2019.12,13

Reporting practices for race and ethnicity varied widely, with roughly half of the articles reporting some measure, a finding that aligns with other recent research on this topic.12,13 When researchers do report race or ethnicity, our results suggest that there is little consensus about best practices. Many articles, especially from the U.S., rely on simplistic distinctions (e.g., Black or white, Hispanic or not), as seen in Fig. 3 and Table 2. Even though U.S. agencies request the use of OMB race and ethnicity categories, very few papers actually did this. Even those categories do not meaningfully reflect human diversity, whether genetics, ancestry, experiences of racism, or any other relevant factor. Researchers face a difficult irony: they are often stuck using categories created by racism to study the effects of racism. Meanwhile, many studies rely on single, simple measures of SES (e.g., a three-tiered variable of education or income). These practices do not capture the cumulative impact of social and environmental exposures over a lifetime, especially given the intersecting effects of racism, poverty, and other social determinants.6,24, 25, 26, 27,29

The findings also differed dramatically by author and participant geography. Three-quarters of studies with a U.S. corresponding author or U.S. research participants reported on race or ethnicity, while under one-third of articles published by non-U.S. authors did. The corresponding authors in our sample reported institutional affiliations in thirty-five unique countries. Although the low numbers of articles from many countries complicates nuanced assessments, articles with U.S. corresponding authors by far reported race or ethnicity at higher rates than other countries. SES data were used at similarly low rates across countries. These gaps could reflect different national guidelines for scientific research (e.g., different guidelines provided by funders or journals about the inclusion of diverse populations, or different standards for how such data should be reported). It would be valuable to conduct further research to analyse the history, content, and scientific justifications of these practices. The ubiquity of race in the U.S. medical literature might also reflect distinct political and social values of U.S. researchers and funders. This merits further investigation as well. Importantly, most studies had no explanation of how data on race or ethnicity was collected, whether by patient self-report, chart review, or provider judgement. This widespread omission also impacts the inter-reliability of using these variables.

Socioeconomic status was not widespread in our sample of the medical literature, a finding consistent with that of other recent research on this topic.12,13 Fewer than one-third of articles reported even a single SES variable. SES reporting also differed significantly by geography, though less dramatically than race or ethnicity. It also varied widely between journals, appearing two- to five-times as often in an epidemiology journal (i.e., AJE) compared to the medical journals. In our sample, SES was reported at a rate of 22.7% across NEJM, JAMA, and The Lancet, which was higher than Alegria et al. (2021) reported in those same journals in 2019 (12.3%). This may reflect our broader sample (e.g., not limited to RCTs) or change over a short time, but overall both analyses found that only a small fraction of published articles reported SES.12

The gap between medicine and epidemiology may relate to the histories of these disciplines: when they diverged in the early twentieth century, clinicians focused on individual patients and their cellular pathophysiology while epidemiologists focused on the social and environmental contexts of illness.30 The fields, however, have since converged, with clinicians showing greater interest in the social determinants of health and epidemiologists studying genetics and molecular biology. Our findings reinforce that most medical researchers, however, have not yet brought SES into their research studies. The epidemiology literature shows that it is possible to do so consistently.

Specifying the age of research participants was nearly ubiquitous in our sample. This is unsurprising: age affects disease risk and treatment outcome. It is certainly important to know whether a study was done in children, young adults, or older adults, and that the age distribution in intervention vs. control groups was equivalent. But is age so much more important than all the other variables that it should be reported more often than the others? How often does knowledge of participants’ age (often reported to three significant digits) influence the interpretation of results? Further research could discern whether the universal reporting of age with such exactness is warranted.

Specifying the mix of males and females is almost as common. However, the majority of articles fail to distinguish between biological sex and gender identity. Very few articles acknowledge patients who fall outside the binary, even though trans and nonbinary patients’ inclusion in studies both potentially impacts their care and acknowledges the validity of their identities. Reliance on a male-female distinction reflects assumptions about which aspects of human diversity (e.g., anatomy or karyotype) matter most. Future studies could more concretely identify the best ways to report on the complexity of human sexual orientation and gender identity—characteristics that also shape disease risk and treatment outcomes.

Researchers have to make complex decisions in their quest to transform human experience into data. They face an admittedly difficult task. They have been asked to take seriously certain aspects of human diversity, but consensus about best practices has constantly been in flux. Further complicating matters, choices for language about race, gender, and identity have become politically charged, and the dynamics of all of this differ in each country. While we acknowledge this challenge, we do believe that researchers could do more than most have been doing: after all, a few of the articles in our sample did exhibit considerable sophistication in their demographic reporting as evidenced in Table 2.

Researchers’ decisions have consequences that extend beyond the reported data. For instance, the frequent inclusion of simplistic markers of race (e.g., merely Black or white) reinforces the notion that these “races” are real in a biological sense, a notion with many harmful effects.3,5,30 Any effort invested in finding better ways to measure and write about human diversity (whether race, ethnicity, sex, gender, or age) should include efforts to characterise and report relevant social determinants.10,24,27,31 Only by doing this will we be able to generate the evidence base required for the precision medicine that so many researchers imagine today. Some researchers do manage to use sophisticated markers, and such practices should be within reach of many more.

Many policy interventions could improve how patient demographics are reported. In 2021, editors of several journals issued new guidelines outlining the responsibilities that researchers have to report gender, ethnicity, and SES as often as they do age, sex, or race.32, 33, 34 Surveys of researchers could probe their decisions about what characteristics to include and why they believe those will be meaningful for the interpretation and application of their findings. Research and clinical registration systems could encode variables on, e.g., race and ethnicity with more precision and specificity than the Black-white or Hispanic-not Hispanic dichotomies in order to capture aspects of identity that are distinct from genetic ancestry.35 This new framework could measure directly the things that race and ethnicity are assumed to represent (e.g., experiences of discrimination; diet or other cultural attributes).

Researchers in a variety of fields have developed increasingly sophisticated tools to infer aspects of SES exposure from other demographic data (e.g., address), such as the Harvard Public Health Disparities Geocoding Project, the Area Deprivation Index from the University of Wisconsin, or the U.K Multiple Deprivation Index. Funding agencies such as the NIH or similar agencies in other countries could issue new guidelines for operationalizing demographic characteristics and enforce them through the grant review process.

Limitations of this study include the small dataset of articles from four journals (three medical and one epidemiological) collected from a single year. This was done to allow a detailed, thorough analysis of each article. Larger studies could be done (more journals, more years) but this would require either massive effort or less nuanced analyses. In addition, the small number of articles from many countries limits the conclusions that can be drawn at the country level.

This study generates many possibilities for follow-up research. Analysing the articles by study design (e.g., randomised clinical trial or observational study), by intervention type, by disease, or by specialty discipline may reveal important variations that could be examined by follow-up studies. Adding comparisons across time and with additional journals could help benchmark progress in this area. Qualitative research could be done to interview researchers and discern the extent to which they control or choose the variables they use in the context of the desires or guidelines of funders, journals, or national regulation, or how their existing data are set up.

Clinicians and researchers need to think critically about their use of sex, gender, race, ethnicity, and SES; to justify their decisions; and to report results in a way that is clear and meaningful.7,36 This is not a call to discard concepts like race, ethnicity, or sex, but to handle them—and other important characteristics—with greater sophistication and consistency. We need to be more intentional about when and how we examine, interpret, and report human diversity. Honouring that goal will help us to ask better questions to understand disease risk and treatment outcomes in ways that will benefit all people.
